title: Restaurant closing checklist for takeout spots
seoTitle: Restaurant closing checklist for takeout spots
description: Use this closing checklist to shut down a takeout restaurant faster, catch missed orders, and prep the phone, kitchen, and front counter.
question: What should I put on a restaurant closing checklist for a takeout restaurant?
answer: A good restaurant closing checklist for a takeout spot should cover orders, phones, kitchen cleanup, cash, inventory, and tomorrow’s setup. It should be short enough that staff can follow it every night, but detailed enough to catch missed tickets, unfinished prep, and messages from callers.
summary: You’ll be able to build a practical closing checklist that fits a takeout restaurant’s phone, kitchen, and front counter.
intro:
A restaurant closing checklist for a takeout spot should cover phones, orders, kitchen cleanup, cash, and tomorrow’s setup. It should be simple enough that the closing team can use it every night without guessing.

For takeout restaurants, closing is not just wiping counters. It is also making sure late phone orders are handled, sold-out items are updated, and tomorrow’s opener is not walking into surprises. If you use [call forwarding codes](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) or an AI phone host like ROAL, the phone side needs its own closing steps too.

sections.h2: What should my restaurant closing checklist cover first?
sections.body:
Start with the parts that can cost you money or cause a bad next-day rush. For a takeout restaurant, that usually means: unanswered calls, open tickets, menu items that ran out, cash drawer count, and prep for the next shift.

Here is a simple order for closing:

1. Check the kitchen screen for any ticket still marked new, preparing, or ready.
2. Make sure every phone order is either handed off, picked up, or marked complete.
3. Remove sold-out items from the menu board, printed menu notes, and your phone menu.
4. Count cash and note delivery app payouts separately from pickup orders.
5. Set out what the opener needs: bags, lids, receipts, sauces, and prep notes.

A useful script for the last caller of the night is: “We’re closing soon. I can take your pickup order now, and we’ll give you the earliest ready time.” That helps the staff stay consistent.

If you use ROAL, it can keep taking pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, answer hours and address questions, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. That makes the closing checklist easier because the last calls are already written down clearly.

sections.h2: How do I close the phone side without missing late orders?
sections.body:
Takeout restaurants lose money when the phone rings after the team gets distracted by cleanup. The fix is to make the phone part of closing as clear as the dining room part.

Use this phone checklist:

- Check whether the line is still being forwarded to the right place.
- Confirm your greeting still matches tonight’s hours.
- Make sure callers hear what is actually available.
- Decide who handles reservations, catering, allergy questions, and complaints after close.
- Save any voicemail or message notes for the opener.

If your restaurant uses call forwarding, confirm the setup with your carrier or phone system. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off. Some mobile carriers use **21*number# to forward all calls and ##21# to turn it off, while **61*number# and **67*number# may handle unanswered or busy calls. Codes vary, so test with a real call before you rely on it.

If you want a cleaner setup, ROAL can answer the restaurant’s phone, take orders from the live menu, and hand tricky calls to staff with a summary. It also keeps call history and transcripts in the dashboard, which is useful when the closing manager wants to see what came in after the rush.

sections.h2: How do I build a kitchen and prep close that actually gets done?
sections.body:
A good kitchen close should be specific to the food you sell. A pizza shop, deli, or family takeout spot all have different end-of-night problems, but the checklist should still be concrete.

Use a fill-in-the-blank version like this:

| Area | What to check |
|---|---|
| Hot line | Turn off equipment, wipe surfaces, label leftovers |
| Cold line | Cover ingredients, date items, rotate anything open |
| Fryers or ovens | Shut down safely, empty crumbs, clean around equipment |
| Packaging | Refill bags, boxes, napkins, forks, and condiments |
| Prep | Note what is low for tomorrow’s first hour |

Example: say your Friday close uses 12 pizza boxes, 8 pasta containers, and 6 sauce cups after 9 p.m. Write that down and compare it with your typical Saturday opener. Then set tomorrow’s prep list from real numbers, not guesses.

A closing line that helps crews move faster is: “Last ticket check, then station wipe-down.” That tells everyone what happens next.

If the kitchen screen shows live tickets, make one person responsible for confirming that no order is left in a strange state. ROAL’s kitchen screen shows new, preparing, and ready tickets, so the closer can scan one place instead of hunting across paper slips and texts.

sections.h2: What cash, order, and report checks belong at closing?
sections.body:
Closing is the time to match what happened during the night with what the drawer and tickets say happened. Do this before everyone goes home.

A simple close-out checklist:

1. Count the register or cash drawer.
2. Separate pickup orders, delivery apps, and any other sales channel you use.
3. Compare completed tickets to the number of meals made.
4. Flag voids, remakes, or comps for the manager.
5. Save the close sheet where the opener can find it.

Worked example: say your average pickup order is $28, and you had 18 completed phone orders. That is $504 in phone-order sales before tips and any other sales channel. Plug in your own average check and order count so you can spot when the night feels off.

A good manager habit is to keep one notebook line for each night: orders taken, issues, and anything the opener must know.

sections.h2: How should I handle sold-out items, FAQs, and tricky calls near closing?
sections.body:
Near close, callers ask the same kinds of questions over and over: what is still available, what time you close, whether parking is open, and whether a dish has an allergen. Your checklist should say who answers those questions and where the answer lives.

Make a short night-shift FAQ sheet with these items:

- Current hours
- Parking or pickup instructions
- Sold-out items
- Allergy-sensitive questions
- Reservation requests
- Manager callbacks

Example script for staff: “We’re out of that item tonight, but I can tell you what is still available.” That is better than guessing or promising something the kitchen cannot make.

ROAL reads menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or uploaded menus, then answers common questions from that live menu. It also does not offer items marked sold out, which helps close time stay cleaner. When a caller asks something it cannot answer, the question lands in an inbox, and the owner answers once so the host knows it from then on.

That means your closing checklist can include one final review step: update any menu change before the last wave of calls. If the special is gone, remove it. If the sauce is limited, note it. Small fixes save a lot of back-and-forth after 8 or 9 p.m.

sections.h2: What should the opener get from the closer every night?
sections.body:
A closing checklist should always end with a handoff. The opener should not have to guess what happened after dinner rush.

Use this handoff list:

- Any orders waiting for pickup
- Any caller messages or callbacks
- Low stock items or prep shortages
- Equipment that needs attention
- Menu items that sold out tonight
- Notes on complaints, catering, or allergy-sensitive calls

A practical handoff note can be as simple as: “Two late pickups completed, wings low, and caller asked about catering for Saturday.” That gives the opener a real starting point.

If you want a cleaner system, ROAL keeps call history with transcripts and recordings in the dashboard, plus live kitchen tickets. That makes it easier to review what came in after the dining room got busy and what still needs follow-up the next morning.

You can also use [your first week with an AI phone host](/blog/what-to-check-in-first-week-ai-host) to set a few house rules for how calls should be handled at close. The goal is to reduce guesswork, not add work. A good handoff should take less than a minute to read and still tell the whole story.

sections.h2: How do I turn this into a checklist my staff will use?
sections.body:
Keep it short, post it where people actually close, and assign one owner for each area. A checklist that is too long gets ignored. A checklist that is too vague gets skipped.

Use this final format:

| Step | Owner | Done |
|---|---|---|
| Final phone check | Manager | ☐ |
| Last ticket review | Kitchen lead | ☐ |
| Sold-out items updated | Shift lead | ☐ |
| Drawer counted | Manager | ☐ |
| Opener handoff written | Closing lead | ☐ |

You can print the checklist, keep it on a clipboard, or turn it into a simple closing sheet on the wall. The best version is the one your team uses every night.

If your restaurant is still relying on voicemail or a rushed end-of-night answering routine, take a look at [AI phone host vs voicemail](/compare/voicemail) and [Pricing](/pricing) to see the difference between a fixed monthly bill and pay-per-order pricing. If you want to test a setup from your own website or menu, [build a free test host](/try).

The checklist should be reviewed after a busy Friday or holiday rush and tightened up when staff notice repeat problems. That way it stays useful for your actual restaurant, not just on paper.

takeaways: Cover phones, tickets, cash, prep, and handoff in one checklist.
Use exact steps and scripts so the closing team does not improvise.
Update sold-out items and hours before the last calls come in.
Give the opener a short written handoff every night.
Use real order counts and average checks when you review closing totals.

faq.q: What should a restaurant closing checklist include for takeout orders?
faq.a: It should include final phone checks, open ticket review, sold-out item updates, cash count, kitchen cleanup, and a handoff for the opener. For takeout restaurants, it should also cover late pickup orders and any caller messages that need follow-up the next day.

faq.q: How do I close the phone line at my restaurant?
faq.a: That depends on your carrier or phone system. Many landlines and some carriers use *72 to forward calls and *73 to turn forwarding off, while some mobile carriers use codes such as **21*number# or ##21#; always confirm with your carrier and test it with a real call. Business VoIP systems usually use a web portal instead of keypad codes.

faq.q: Should I keep taking orders near closing time?
faq.a: Yes, if your kitchen can still handle them and you are clear about the ready time. A simple script like “We’re closing soon, but I can take your pickup order now” helps set expectations. If you use a phone host, make sure it only offers items still available and sends the order to the kitchen cleanly.

faq.q: How can I make closing easier when the phone is busy?
faq.a: Use a short closing checklist and assign one person to the phone, one to the kitchen close, and one to the cash or handoff notes. If you use ROAL, it can answer routine questions, take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen so staff can focus on closing.
